conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me where the pain is and how long it’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s mostly on the right side, and also up in the middle and kind of low, like suprapubic. It’s been about four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How severe was it at its worst, and is anything making it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was really bad at first. It gets better if I just lie still. Moving makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting? Any change from your usual nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I always have some nausea and I take Zofran in the morning. It’s not really worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. With your Roux-en-Y history and the G-tube, we want to make sure there’s no blockage or other complication. For now we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—and give IV fluids. We’ll also pause your tube feeds temporarily while we evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stopping the tube feeds worries me. I get low blood sugar if I don’t have them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important point. We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely while feeds are off, and we’ll restart feeds as soon as it’s safe. The goal is to avoid worsening pain or nausea while we check what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you thinking it’s an obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s on the list of possibilities given your anatomy after bypass, but it’s not the only possibility. We’re going to use labs and imaging to look for signs of obstruction or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What tests are you ordering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check bloodwork—things like blood counts, electrolytes, kidney and liver tests, and lipase. And we’re planning a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT be through my tube or by mouth? I can’t tolerate much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can do it without oral contrast. The CT uses IV contrast, and we’ll coordinate the best approach given your tube and your tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My incision still needs packing too. It’s been a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue daily wound care here—packing and dressing changes—and we’ll check the area each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for pain? It’s not as bad as earlier, but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll treat your pain and nausea while we work this up. We’ll avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my labs show anything scary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far, your labs look reassuring—no big signs of infection, and your kidney function and electrolytes look okay. We’ll keep trending them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I get the CT results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As soon as radiology finalizes the read, I’ll come back and go over it with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have your CT results. The scan shows your Roux-en-Y anatomy and the G-tube in the excluded part of the stomach, and importantly there’s no evidence of small bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no dilated bowel loops and no obstruction seen. The scan also notes your midline incision with packing material, and there isn’t fat stranding around it on CT, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Abdominal pain can still happen even without an obstruction—sometimes from irritation, inflammation that doesn’t show clearly on imaging, or sensitivity around prior surgical sites. The good news is we don’t see an emergency surgical blockage. Our plan is supportive care: rest the gut briefly, control pain and nausea, and then restart feeds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start my tube feeds tonight? I’m worried about hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart gradually rather than jump to your full home rate. Tonight we’ll keep you on IV fluids and monitor sugars, and we’ll begin a slow feed advancement as your symptoms allow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your pain overnight? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is better if I don’t move much. Nausea is about the same as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Since the CT didn’t show obstruction and you’re stable, we’ll start tube feeds at a low rate and increase stepwise toward your baseline as long as pain and nausea stay controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the goal rate again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your baseline is 60 mL per hour. We’ll work up to that gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The dressing change hurts. Is the wound infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s uncomfortable. Right now, we’re doing daily packing and dressing changes. The imaging didn’t show concerning changes around the incision, and you don’t have fever or lab signs suggesting infection. We’ll keep checking it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the enteral nutrition infusion today. Let us know right away if the feeds worsen your pain, cause bloating, or increase nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If I feel crampy, should I stop it myself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t adjust it on your own—call the nurse. We can pause or slow it safely and assess you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tolerating the feeds so far. Still some pain, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll continue to advance the rate slowly. We’ll also keep your nausea controlled with your usual regimen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in: how are you feeling with the tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The nausea is not worse. Pain is there but not like when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep advancing toward 60 mL/hr. If you stay stable at goal, we can start planning for discharge with home services for wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to drink water by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can allow small sips as tolerated, but the main nutrition will remain through the tube feeds. If anything increases nausea or pain, we’ll scale back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the pain will come back once I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled on a safe home plan, and we’ll give you clear return precautions—like fever, worsening severe pain, vomiting, bloating, or drainage changes from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue rifaximin. We’re also planning lansoprazole twice daily and sucralfate for stomach protection, plus docusate to prevent constipation. For pain, hydromorphone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the stomach medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history after bypass and prior ulcer issues, we want to reduce irritation and protect the lining. Lansoprazole reduces acid, and sucralfate coats and protects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m at a higher feed rate now and it’s okay. When do I hit my normal 60?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you continue tolerating it overnight, we should be able to reach 60 mL/hr by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re at goal tube feeds—60 mL/hr—and your pain and nausea are controlled. That’s what we needed to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge today with home services to help with wound packing and dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for with the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or come back if you get fever over 101.5, redness or swelling around the incision, foul-smelling or colorful drainage, or if the pain suddenly worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I can’t tolerate the feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop severe nausea or vomiting, abdominal bloating, or you can’t keep feeds running, you should call your surgeon’s office right away or return to the emergency department—especially given your risk of hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you review the pain medicine? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hydromorphone is only as needed for pain, every 4 hours if required. Use the lowest amount that controls your pain. It can cause constipation, so take the docusate, and avoid driving or alcohol while using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—just confirming I shouldn’t take anything like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Stick to the plan we’re prescribing and call if you’re unsure about any over-the-counter medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: your discharge diagnosis is PO intolerance with tube feed adjustment. You came in with abdominal pain and nausea, we ruled out obstruction on CT, rested your gut briefly, then advanced tube feeds back to goal while continuing daily wound care. Do you have any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that makes sense. I’m relieved the CT didn’t show a blockage. I’ll follow the instructions and call if anything changes.
